passage.title: Breaking the Silence of Stone
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Bank
passage.text:
For more than a thousand years, no living person could read the carved temple walls of Egypt. Scholars were baffled by the rows of birds, reeds, lions, and eyes known as hieroglyphs. Most thinkers assumed that each tiny picture stood only for a whole idea, such as a hawk meaning swiftness. They looked only for pure picture symbols on the stone walls. As a result, they could not link the carvings to any spoken tongue. That long silence began to break in 1799 when soldiers near the port of Rosetta dug up a heavy slab of dark rock.

The broken stone held the same royal decree carved in three scripts so priests, clerks, and rulers could all read it. Because scholars already knew the ancient Greek letters in the bottom band, they held a vital key to the upper texts. On the dark slab of stone, the royal names sealed inside oval rings were matched by Thomas Young to Greek letters at the bottom. Young proved that foreign rulers' names, such as Ptolemy, were spelled out by sound using bird and lion signs. Yet Young soon stopped short, believing that Egyptians used sound signs only when writing foreign names.

Across the channel in France, a young scholar named Jean-François Champollion suspected the system went much deeper. Unlike Young, Champollion had spent years learning Coptic, the late church language passed down from ancient Egyptian speech. He wondered whether native Egyptian words on temple walls also hid spoken sounds alongside picture signs. In 1822, he received fresh copies of oval name rings carved at an older temple far up the Nile.

The first sign inside one ring was a small circle with a dot, the Coptic symbol for the sun, pronounced "Ra." Next stood a reed hook and two folded cloths that Young had already linked to the "m" and "s" sounds. Putting the idea of the sun together with those two sound signs, Champollion read the famous native pharaoh's name: Ramses. At once, he saw that the script was a clever hybrid of sound letters and meaning signs.

To decipher a full line, a reader had to blend spoken syllables with silent clue pictures placed at the ends of words. For example, a scribe might first spell an action word by its sound. Then the writer would add a tiny pair of walking legs to show motion. By uniting Young's sound chart with his own Coptic speech clues, Champollion unlocked three thousand years of history.

tier2Words.definition: Something made by combining two different systems or elements

tier2Words.definition: To convert a hidden or ancient script into understandable language

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"On the dark slab of stone, the royal names sealed inside oval rings were matched by Thomas Young to Greek letters at the bottom."

Who performed the action of matching the royal names in this sentence?

options.text: The oval rings that sealed the royal names on the stone
options.childFeedback: The oval rings were just the carved borders around the royal names on the stone; stone carvings cannot match things by themselves.

options.text: The Greek letters carved at the bottom of the dark slab
options.childFeedback: The Greek letters at the bottom were what Thomas Young matched the royal rings to, not the scholar doing the matching.

options.text: Thomas Young, who compared the rings with the Greek letters
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the passive phrase 'were matched by Thomas Young to Greek letters at the bottom' shows that Thomas Young performed the action of matching the royal names.

options.text: The priests and clerks who carved the three scripts
options.childFeedback: Ancient priests and clerks read the decree thousands of years ago, whereas Thomas Young was the modern scholar who matched the rings to the Greek text.

questions.provingSentenceText: On the dark slab of stone, the royal names sealed inside oval rings were matched by Thomas Young to Greek letters at the bottom.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the passive phrase 'were matched by Thomas Young to Greek letters at the bottom' shows that Thomas Young performed the action of matching the royal names.
questions.parentExplanation: The subject 'the royal names' receives the action 'were matched.' The agent performing the matching is introduced by 'by Thomas Young.'
questions.retryHint: Check the words right after 'matched by' in the Paragraph 2 sentence to see who compared the oval rings with the Greek letters.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"At once, he saw that the script was a clever hybrid of sound letters and meaning signs."

What does the word "hybrid" most nearly mean as used in this sentence?

options.text: A blend that combines two different methods
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'hybrid' means a blend that combines two different methods, because Egyptian hieroglyphs combined spoken sound letters with symbolic meaning signs.

options.text: A mistake carved by an untrained scribe
options.childFeedback: The sentence calls the script 'a clever hybrid,' showing it was a smart, purposeful system rather than a scribe's mistake.

options.text: A royal law written only for foreign kings
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, Champollion is reading the native Egyptian pharaoh's name 'Ramses,' proving the system was not just for foreign kings.

options.text: A secret language that can never be spoken aloud
options.childFeedback: Champollion used spoken Coptic sounds like 'Ra' along with 'm' and 's' to read the words aloud, so it was definitely a spoken language.

questions.provingSentenceText: At once, he saw that the script was a clever hybrid of sound letters and meaning signs.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'hybrid' means a blend that combines two different methods, because Egyptian hieroglyphs combined spoken sound letters with symbolic meaning signs.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 4, Champollion combines the solar symbol ('Ra') with phonetic consonant signs ('m' and 's'), proving that hieroglyphs are a 'hybrid' (combination) of ideograms and phonetic letters.
questions.retryHint: Look at the words right after 'hybrid' in Paragraph 4 ('of sound letters and meaning signs') to see the two things being combined.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 2, what kept Thomas Young from decoding the entire Egyptian writing system?

options.text: He could not read any of the ancient Greek letters carved at the bottom of the Rosetta Stone.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 states that scholars already knew the ancient Greek letters in the bottom band, which is how Young matched Ptolemy's name.

options.text: He assumed that Egyptians used phonetic sound signs only when spelling foreign rulers' names.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 explains that after spelling out foreign names like Ptolemy, Thomas Young stopped short because he mistakenly believed Egyptians used sound signs only for foreign names.

options.text: The oval rings containing Ptolemy's name had been completely chipped off the stone slab.
options.childFeedback: Ptolemy's name was still on the stone—Paragraph 2 says Young proved Ptolemy was spelled out by sound using bird and lion signs.

options.text: He refused to study the bird and lion signs inside the royal rings.
options.childFeedback: Young specifically studied the bird and lion signs inside the oval rings to prove how Ptolemy's name was spelled by sound.

questions.provingSentenceText: Yet Young soon stopped short, believing that Egyptians used sound signs only when writing foreign names.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 2 explains that after spelling out foreign names like Ptolemy, Thomas Young stopped short because he mistakenly believed Egyptians used sound signs only for foreign names.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 states that although Young proved foreign names like Ptolemy were spelled phonetically, he 'stopped short, believing that Egyptians used sound signs only when writing foreign names.'
questions.retryHint: Read the last sentence of Paragraph 2 to see the mistaken belief that made Thomas Young stop short.

questions.prompt: How did Champollion's background knowledge allow him to go further than Thomas Young in Paragraphs 3 and 4?

options.text: Champollion had dug up the Rosetta Stone himself while serving as a soldier in 1799.
options.childFeedback: Soldiers near the port of Rosetta dug up the stone in 1799 (Paragraph 1), whereas Champollion was a scholar in France studying copies of inscriptions.

options.text: He proved that every hieroglyph on Egyptian temple walls was a silent picture with zero spoken sounds.
options.childFeedback: Champollion proved the exact opposite: native Egyptian hieroglyphs included spoken phonetic sounds alongside meaning pictures.

options.text: His knowledge of Coptic allowed him to connect the sun symbol's spoken sound ('Ra') with Young's phonetic 'm' and 's' signs to read native Egyptian words.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 3 and 4 explain that because Champollion knew Coptic, he knew the Egyptian word for the sun symbol was pronounced 'Ra,' letting him combine it with Young's 'm' and 's' sounds to read 'Ramses.'

options.text: He translated the Greek band at the bottom of the stone before Thomas Young ever saw it.
options.childFeedback: Scholars already knew the Greek letters from the start, and Champollion built on Thomas Young's earlier sound chart rather than working before Young.

questions.provingSentenceText: Putting the idea of the sun together with those two sound signs, Champollion read the famous native pharaoh's name: Ramses.
questions.childTip: Paragraphs 3 and 4 explain that because Champollion knew Coptic, he knew the Egyptian word for the sun symbol was pronounced 'Ra,' letting him combine it with Young's 'm' and 's' sounds to read 'Ramses.'
questions.parentExplanation: Synthesizing Paragraphs 3 and 4 shows that Champollion's mastery of Coptic gave him the spoken word for the sun ('Ra'), which he combined with Young's phonetic 'm' and 's' signs to decode the native name 'Ramses.'
questions.retryHint: Connect what Champollion had spent years learning in Paragraph 3 with how he read the first sign ('Ra') inside the ring in Paragraph 4.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Ancient Egyptian scribes used walking legs at the end of every word to confuse foreign soldiers.
options.childFeedback: The tiny pair of walking legs in Paragraph 5 was added only to action words to show motion—and it helped readers understand the word rather than confuse soldiers.

options.text: Cracking the Rosetta Stone required realizing that hieroglyphs blend spoken sound signs with symbolic meaning pictures.
options.childFeedback: Across the passage, the central idea is that scholars finally decoded Egyptian hieroglyphs when Champollion realized the script blends spoken sound signs with silent meaning pictures.

options.text: The Rosetta Stone was the only stone slab ever discovered near a port in Egypt.
options.childFeedback: The passage never claims the Rosetta Stone was the only stone slab ever found in Egypt; in fact, Paragraph 3 mentions carvings from an older temple up the Nile.

options.text: Coptic was much easier for European scholars to read than ancient Greek.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 states that scholars already knew ancient Greek easily, whereas Champollion had to spend years studying Coptic.

questions.provingSentenceText: To decipher a full line, a reader had to blend spoken syllables with silent clue pictures placed at the ends of words.
questions.childTip: Across the passage, the central idea is that scholars finally decoded Egyptian hieroglyphs when Champollion realized the script blends spoken sound signs with silent meaning pictures.
questions.parentExplanation: The central idea across all five paragraphs is that scholars failed when looking only for pure symbols, and succeeded once Young and Champollion proved hieroglyphs combine phonetic syllables with ideographic clue pictures.
questions.retryHint: Look at the last sentence of Paragraph 4 and the first sentence of Paragraph 5 to see the key discovery that unlocked hieroglyphs.
